reasons: Lake identity records the case as United States v. Hamza Kolsuz, court 4th Cir. 2018, docket 16-4687, decided 2018-05-18.
Lake citation display and selected official citation are 890 F.3d 133, matching the asserted reporter citation.
The opinion states that agents subjected the phone to a month-long, off-site forensic analysis yielding a nearly 900-page report.
The opinion states the forensic analysis was properly categorized as a border search despite temporal and spatial distance from the airport.
The opinion states that under Riley the forensic examination must be considered a nonroutine border search requiring some measure of individualized suspicion.
The opinion expressly declines to decide whether reasonable suspicion is enough or whether a warrant based on probable cause is required.

The opinion affirms because agents reasonably relied on precedent allowing warrantless border searches of digital devices based on at least reasonable suspicion, making suppression inappropriate under the good-faith exception.
The opinion frames the appeal around whether the forensic phone search was justified under the border search exception.
The case resolves that the forensic phone search was a border search and that, after Riley, forensic phone searches are nonroutine border searches requiring individualized suspicion.
residual_risks: The label Key is editorial, but the disclosed opinion supports central relevance to the Border Searches home.
